idiom_name: prototype methods returning `this` (jQuery) or a new value per step (Array methods, Promise.prototype.then)
implementation_notes: JavaScript chains through ordinary methods that return this - jQuery's whole API is built on it and its documentation marks chainability by the return type - or through methods that return a new value, which is how the language's own types behave: Array.prototype.filter/map/slice return new arrays, so `users.filter(...).map(...)` composes without mutation, and Promise.prototype.then returns a new promise so a chain threads values and rejections through one expression with a single catch at the end. Nothing in the language is needed beyond returning the receiver or the next value; the classic `return this` form fits imperative wrapper APIs, the value-returning form fits transformations, and mixing the two in one API is what makes call sites ambiguous. What replaces the classic builder structure here is often just an options object with destructuring defaults, unless the task really is a step-by-step grammar.
code_sketch:
$('#panel').addClass('open').fadeIn(200).delay(500).fadeOut();     // each call returns the jQuery object
const names = users.filter(u => u.active).map(u => u.name);       // new array per step, no mutation
fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(render).catch(report);        // promise chain: values and errors thread through
pitfalls: A step that returns a queried value instead of the receiver ends the chain silently - jQuery's .html()/.text()/.val() return content - so the next link either throws or misbehaves only at runtime.

A mutating chain over shared state (the DOM, or `this` inside a constructor) hides changes; passing a step as a callback loses the intended `this`, and arrow functions do not repair a chain designed around dynamic this.

Without static types a mistyped step yields undefined and the failure surfaces far away; in a promise chain every rejection must be caught (a trailing .catch, or await in a try block) or it becomes an unhandled rejection.
